sources.name: Quintus Fabius Pictor

works.books: Number of books unknown; c. 30 fragments and testimonia, plus a Taormina library inscription summarizing him
works.note: Ran from Aeneas and the foundation to the Second Punic War, which he lived through.

sources.reliability: The first Roman historian, a senator writing in Greek to explain Rome to the Hellenistic world during the Hannibalic war. Polybius used him for the Punic Wars and criticized his pro-Roman, anti-Barcid bias (Polyb. 1.14-15, 3.8-9). Dated Rome's founding to 748/747 BC.
sources.summary: Senator of the great Fabian gens, sent to consult Delphi after Cannae (216). Founder of Roman annalistic historiography; all later accounts of early Rome descend in part from him.

sources.name: Lucius Cincius Alimentus
sources.reliability: Praetor 210 BC, once a prisoner of Hannibal, who told him he had lost 36,000 men since the Rhône (Livy 21.38). Fragments few but valuable for eyewitness data.
sources.summary: Second Roman annalist in Greek; dated the foundation to 729/728 BC.

sources.name: Gnaeus Naevius

works.books: Saturnian epic, later divided into 7 books; c. 60 fragments
works.note: Opened with the Aeneas legend before the war itself.

sources.reliability: A veteran of the First Punic War writing epic about it; fragments are tiny and mostly grammarians' citations.
sources.summary: Campanian poet; first Latin national epic. Jailed for attacking the Metelli.

sources.name: Quintus Ennius

works.books: 18 books of hexameters; c. 600 lines survive in quotation
works.note: From the fall of Troy to the 170s BC; books 7-9 on the Second Punic War; book 16 added for the Istrian war.

sources.reliability: Epic not history, but deeply influential on Roman self-image (moribus antiquis res stat Romana virisque); Cicero, Virgil and Livy drew on it. Fragmentary.
sources.summary: Messapian-born poet brought to Rome by Cato (204), protégé of Fulvius Nobilior, whom he accompanied to Ambracia (189).

sources.name: Cato the Elder

works.note: Books 1-3 on the origins of Rome and the Italian peoples; 4-5 the Punic Wars; 6-7 down to 149, with his own speeches inserted. Famously omitted generals' names.
Oldest surviving Latin prose work: villa slave management, contracts, recipes, rituals.
Over 150 speeches known to Cicero; c. 80 attested by title, including Pro Rhodiensibus (167) and De sumptu suo.

sources.reliability: First Latin prose history; strong personal and anti-aristocratic slant. De agri cultura is a primary document for 2nd-century slave agriculture.
sources.summary: Novus homo from Tusculum, consul 195, censor 184, implacable advocate of destroying Carthage (Carthago delenda est).

sources.name: Polybius

works.books: 40 books; books 1-5 complete (to Cannae), the rest in Byzantine excerpts (Constantinian Excerpta, Codex Urbinas) and fragments
works.note: Main theme: how Rome conquered the known world in under 53 years (220-167); books 1-2 background from 264; extended to 146. Book 6 analyses the Roman constitution and army; book 12 attacks Timaeus; book 34 geography.

sources.reliability: Best surviving historian of the Middle Republic: a cavalry commander, hostage, friend of Scipio Aemilianus, present at Carthage in 146. Used documents (the Carthage treaties, the Lacinian inscription of Hannibal for troop numbers), walked Hannibal's route, interrogated eyewitnesses. Biases: pro-Scipionic, pro-Achaean; tendency to systematize causes (pragmatic history).
sources.summary: Achaean statesman from Megalopolis, deported to Rome among 1,000 hostages after Pydna (167). Livy followed him closely for eastern affairs.

sources.name: Valerius Antias
sources.reliability: Notorious for inflated casualty figures, as Livy complains (Livy 33.10, 36.38); a key Sullan-era annalist behind Livy's third and fourth decades.
sources.summary: Late annalist of the 70s BC; the archetype of rhetorical, invented 'annalistic' detail.

sources.name: Quintus Claudius Quadrigarius

works.note: Began with the Gallic sack, deliberately skipping the unverifiable earlier period.

sources.reliability: Livy used him heavily in books 6-10 and 30-45; more sober than Antias but still rhetorical. Gellius preserved his vivid Torquatus single-combat passage.
sources.summary: Sullan-era annalist.

sources.name: Posidonius

works.note: Continued Polybius; probably ended with the 80s BC.

sources.reliability: Stoic polymath from Apamea whose lost Histories underlie much of Diodorus, Strabo, Athenaeus and Plutarch on the Sicilian slave wars, the Gauls (head-hunting, druids), the Cimbri and Athenion's Athens.
sources.summary: Head of the Stoic school at Rhodes; envoy to Marius; host to Cicero and Pompey.

sources.name: Sallust

works.note: Includes speeches of Caesar and Cato in the debate of 5 Dec 63.
Background from Micipsa's death (118); war 111-105.

works.books: 5 books; c. 500 fragments, with complete speeches and letters (Lepidus, Philippus, Cotta, Macer, Pompey's letter, Mithridates' letter)

sources.reliability: Brilliant, Thucydidean stylist with a moralizing scheme of decline after 146 and hostility to the nobility; chronology and geography in the Jugurtha are loose. A Caesarian partisan, expelled from the Senate in 50, governor of Africa Nova (46) and enriched there.
sources.summary: The first great Roman historical monographer; tribune 52. His gardens (Horti Sallustiani) became imperial property.

sources.name: Julius Caesar

works.note: One book per campaigning year: Helvetii and Ariovistus (58) to Alesia (52).
Ends with Caesar besieged in Alexandria (late 48).

sources.reliability: Eyewitness commander's account in plain third-person prose; indispensable but self-serving (casualty figures for enemies, e.g. 368,000 Helvetii and 430,000 Usipetes and Tencteri, are suspect; the Gallic ethnography of book 6 is partly schematic). Cicero praised the style; Asinius Pollio doubted its accuracy.
sources.summary: Wrote the Gallic commentaries probably year by year or in 52/51 as political dispatches; the civil-war books are an apologia.

sources.name: Caesarian corpus (Hirtius and continuators)

works.note: Bellovaci, Uxellodunum.
Probably Hirtius; Alexandria, Pharnaces at Zela, Illyricum, Spain.
Anonymous officer's eyewitness account of Thapsus.
Anonymous, crude Latin; campaign of Munda (17 Mar 45); text breaks off.

sources.reliability: Completes Caesar's narrative from 51 to 45. The Bellum Africum and Hispaniense are valuable as unpolished soldiers' accounts.
sources.summary: Aulus Hirtius (consul 43, killed at Mutina) wrote BG 8 and probably the Alexandrine War; the others are by unknown Caesarian officers.

sources.name: Cicero

works.t: Letters (Ad Atticum, Ad Familiares, Ad Quintum fratrem, Ad Brutum)
works.books: c. 900 letters (some 90 from correspondents); Att. 16 books (68-44), Fam. 16 books (62-43), QFr. 3 books (60-54), Brut. 2 books (43)
works.note: Thin before 61; dense 51-43.

works.books: 58 survive complete or in part (of c. 88 known), from Pro Quinctio (81) to the 14 Philippics (44-43)
works.note: Verrines (70), Catilinarians (63), Pro Sestio (56), Pro Milone (52) and others.
Brutus (46) is a history of Roman oratory from the beginnings; De re publica (54-51, partly recovered from a Vatican palimpsest) and De legibus on the constitution; De officiis (44).

sources.reliability: The single richest body of evidence for any period of antiquity: day-by-day, unguarded correspondence for 61-43 BC. Speeches are advocacy, not fact; letters reveal motives but reflect Cicero's own vanity and anxieties. Asconius and the scholia supply context.
sources.summary: Novus homo from Arpinum, consul 63 (Catilinarian conspiracy), exiled 58-57, proconsul of Cilicia 51-50, proscribed and killed 7 Dec 43.

sources.name: Cornelius Nepos

works.t: De viris illustribus: Foreign generals; Hamilcar; Hannibal
works.note: 23 lives of foreign generals survive, including Hamilcar and Hannibal (the only ancient biography of Hannibal).
Atticus written by a friend; Cato in a short version.
Universal chronicle in 3 books, dedicatee of Catullus' poems.

sources.reliability: Uncritical and slight, but the Hannibal preserves non-Polybian material, and the Atticus is a contemporary portrait of a banker-equestrian.
sources.summary: Transpadane friend of Cicero, Atticus and Catullus.

sources.name: Varro

works.note: Written c. 47-43 BC; preserves archaic legal and religious formulae and Roman topography.
Farming, livestock, villa economics (aviaries, fishponds).
41 books; known through Augustine's City of God.

sources.reliability: The Republic's greatest scholar; his antiquarian framework (including the 'Varronian' foundation date of 753 BC) underlies later Roman chronology and religion.
sources.summary: Pompeian legate in Spain (49), pardoned by Caesar and made head of the planned public library; proscribed by Antony but saved.

sources.name: Diodorus Siculus

works.books: 40 books; 1-5 (myth and ethnography) and 11-20 (480-302 BC) complete; 21-40 in fragments and Byzantine excerpts
works.note: Books 21-40 preserve, via excerpts, the Pyrrhic, Punic and Sicilian slave wars and the late Republic to 60 BC; Roman events from the 5th-4th century in books 11-20 give an independent (sometimes earlier) consul list.

sources.reliability: A compiler who reproduces his sources (Ephorus, Timaeus, Hieronymus, Polybius, Posidonius) with little critique, which makes him valuable for lost material; chronology often confused by forcing events into single archon-consul years.
sources.summary: Sicilian from Agyrium, wrote in Rome c. 60-30 BC.

sources.name: Dionysius of Halicarnassus

works.books: 20 books; 1-10 complete, 11 mostly, the rest in excerpts
works.note: From the earliest inhabitants to the outbreak of the First Punic War. Books 1-2 on origins and the regal constitution; 3-11 the kings and early Republic in great detail.

sources.reliability: Argues Romans were really Greeks. Long invented speeches; but preserves antiquarian detail (e.g. the 'Servian' centuriate system, early census figures, the Foedus Cassianum) from Varro and the annalists. Parallel to Livy 1-10.
sources.summary: Greek rhetor who lived in Rome from 30 BC; also wrote literary criticism.

sources.name: Livy

works.books: 142 books; 1-10 and 21-45 survive (41 and 43-45 with gaps), plus a palimpsest fragment of book 91 (Sertorius, 77 BC); the rest known from the Periochae, Oxyrhynchus epitome and fragments
works.note: Ended with the death of Drusus (9 BC). First decade to 293; third decade the Hannibalic war; fourth and fifth to Pydna and 167.

sources.reliability: The main narrative of Republican Rome. For the early period he admits the unreliability of his sources (6.1) and follows the late annalists (Antias, Quadrigarius, Licinius Macer, Tubero); for 218-167 he relies on Polybius for the East, giving high reliability. Preserves annual records (prodigies, magistrates, colonies, temple dedications) from the pontifical tradition. Patriotic, moralizing, militarily vague.
sources.summary: From Patavium; wrote under Augustus, who called him a 'Pompeian' but remained friendly; encouraged the young Claudius to write history.

sources.name: Periochae of Livy

works.note: Valuable for the lost books 11-20 (293-219) and 46-142 (167-9 BC); some entries are a line or two.
Papyrus epitome of books 37-40 and 48-55 with consular dating.

sources.reliability: Uneven and sometimes garbled, but the only continuous outline for much of 293-219 and 167-9 BC, including census returns and key laws.
sources.summary: Anonymous epitome, probably 3rd-4th century; derived from an earlier digest of Livy that also fed Florus, Eutropius, Orosius, Obsequens and Cassiodorus.

sources.name: Fasti Capitolini

works.note: Marble lists of consuls, dictators, magistri equitum, censors and consular tribunes; about two-thirds survive, with gaps (e.g. much of the 3rd century BC).
Triumphs from Romulus to L. Cornelius Balbus (19 BC), the last triumph by a non-imperial general.

sources.reliability: The official Augustan version of Republican chronology (Varronian, with inserted 'dictator years'); early entries are reconstructions, not contemporary records. Found in the Forum from 1546, now in the Capitoline Museums.
sources.summary: Inscribed c. 18-17 BC, probably on the Parthian arch of Augustus in the Forum (or the Regia), with later additions.

sources.name: Res Gestae Divi Augusti

works.note: Copies from Ancyra (Monumentum Ancyranum, Latin and Greek), Apollonia and Antioch in Pisidia; the original stood on bronze pillars before the Mausoleum.

sources.reliability: Augustus' own account of his honours, expenditures (e.g. 860 million sesterces for veterans' land, 600 million in Italy and 260 million in the provinces; 170 million to the aerarium militare) and achievements. Accurate in its numbers but artful in omission (no mention of Antony by name, of the proscriptions, or of Varus).
sources.summary: Written by Augustus and deposited with the Vestals with his will; finalized AD 14.

sources.name: Strabo

works.note: Describes the oikoumene c. 20 BC-AD 23 with historical excursuses back to Homer; books 3-6 on Iberia, Gaul, Britain and Italy, 12-14 Asia Minor, 16-17 the Near East and Egypt.
Continued Polybius.

sources.reliability: Uses Polybius, Posidonius, Artemidorus and personal travel (Egypt with Aelius Gallus). Indispensable for the Augustan empire's geography and client kingdoms; dated for some regions (e.g. Spain via Posidonius).
sources.summary: From Amaseia in Pontus, of a family of Mithridatic courtiers.

sources.name: Velleius Paterculus

works.books: 2 books; book 1 has a large gap from Romulus to 168 BC; book 2 complete
works.note: Book 2 runs from 146 BC to AD 30 and dwells on Tiberius' campaigns in Germany and Pannonia (AD 4-12), in which Velleius served.

sources.reliability: Panegyric of Tiberius and Sejanus written in AD 30; eyewitness value for AD 4-12 (Pannonian revolt, Varus). Lists Roman colonies with dates (1.14-15) and digressions on literary history.
sources.summary: Equestrian cavalry prefect, legate under Tiberius, praetor AD 15.

sources.name: Valerius Maximus

works.note: Organized by theme (religion, omens, discipline, censorial severity, cruelty); epitomized by Julius Paris and Nepotianus.

sources.reliability: Rhetorical handbook of exempla dedicated to Tiberius; unreliable as narrative, but preserves anecdotes and customs from lost Republican sources.
sources.summary: Client of Sextus Pompeius (cos. AD 14).

sources.name: Asconius

works.books: Commentaries on 5 speeches survive (In Pisonem, Pro Scauro, Pro Milone, Pro Cornelio, In toga candida)
works.note: Pro Milone commentary gives the fullest account of Clodius' murder (18 Jan 52) and Pompey's sole consulship.

sources.reliability: Highly reliable scholarly commentary using the acta diurna and senatorial records; corrects Cicero's tendentious statements.
sources.summary: Paduan scholar, wrote c. AD 54-57 for his sons.

sources.name: Granius Licinianus

works.note: Covers the 160s, 105 (Arausio) and 88-78 (Sulla, Lepidus).

sources.reliability: Antiquarian epitomator; the palimpsest (British Library, discovered 1853) gives unique details for the 80s-70s BC.
sources.summary: Probably Antonine-era.

sources.name: Julius Obsequens

works.note: List of prodigies year by year (only 190-11 BC survives), excerpted from Livy.

sources.reliability: Mechanical but faithful excerpt of Livy's prodigy lists, preserving year-entries from lost books (e.g. 166-11 BC).
sources.summary: Probably a 4th-century pagan compiler.

sources.name: Lucan

works.note: Caesar's crossing of the Rubicon to Alexandria.

sources.reliability: Epic of Caesar's war, anti-Caesarian and Republican in sentiment; history bent for effect (Cato's African march, Erichtho the witch), but reflects Neronian views of the civil war.
sources.summary: Nephew of Seneca; forced to suicide after the Pisonian conspiracy.

sources.name: Silius Italicus

works.books: 17 books, the longest surviving Latin epic
works.note: The Second Punic War, following Livy's third decade.

sources.reliability: Derivative of Livy with mythological machinery; of literary rather than historical value.
sources.summary: Consul 68, the last consul appointed by Nero; proconsul of Asia.

sources.name: Frontinus

works.note: Written as curator aquarum (97): capacity, history and abuses of the nine aqueducts, with quinariae figures.
Collection of stratagems, including Domitian's Chattan war (83) in which he served.

sources.reliability: Technical and administrative document of high value on the water supply; the Strategemata is anecdotal.
sources.summary: Consul three times, governor of Britain (c. 74-77, conquered the Silures).

sources.name: Josephus

works.note: From the Maccabees to the fall of Masada (73/74); a detailed description of the Roman army (3.70-109).

works.books: 20 books; books 11-20 cover the Persian-Roman period
works.note: Books 1-10 biblical history. Long excursus on Gaius' death and Claudius' accession (19.1-273) from a Roman source.

sources.reliability: Eyewitness, first as rebel commander in Galilee (surrendered at Jotapata, 67), then on Titus' staff at the siege of Jerusalem (70). Pro-Flavian and self-justifying; numbers inflated (1.1 million dead at Jerusalem), but invaluable; quotes Roman decrees for the Jews.
sources.summary: Jewish priest and aristocrat, freed by Vespasian and given citizenship and a pension in Rome.

sources.name: Philo of Alexandria

works.note: Eyewitness of the Alexandrian pogrom of 38 and his embassy to Caligula (39/40).

sources.reliability: Partisan but vivid primary account of Caligula's court and the persecution under the prefect Flaccus.
sources.summary: Leader of the Alexandrian Jewish community and philosopher.

sources.name: Pliny the Elder

works.note: Encyclopedia with countless historical notices: provincial and city lists (books 3-6, from Augustan documents), mines, prices, metals, art, the census of AD 47 in Italy's 8th region; historical anecdotes from all periods.
Used by Tacitus.
History of his own times continuing Aufidius Bassus; a source for Tacitus' Histories and Annals.

sources.reliability: Uncritical compiler (from some 2,000 volumes), but his geographical books preserve Agrippa's measurements and Augustan administrative lists.
sources.summary: Equestrian officer and procurator; prefect of the fleet at Misenum; died at Stabiae in the eruption of Vesuvius (24 Aug or Oct 79).

sources.name: Pliny the Younger

works.note: Senatorial life, trials (Marius Priscus, 100), villas, the eruption of Vesuvius (6.16, 6.20).
Governor of Bithynia-Pontus: aqueducts, fire brigades, Christians (10.96-97).
Consular speech of thanks, 1 Sep 100.

sources.reliability: Literary letters selected for publication, but book 10 is a unique run of real administrative correspondence between a governor and the emperor.
sources.summary: Nephew and adopted son of the Elder Pliny; consul 100; died in Bithynia c. 113.

sources.name: Tacitus

works.books: 16 (or 18) books; 1-4, part of 5, 6, and 11-16 (broken off in 66) survive
works.note: Lost: Caligula, early Claudius (37-47) and the end of Nero (66-68).

works.books: Originally c. 12-14 books; 1-4 and part of 5 survive
works.note: The year of the four emperors, the Batavian revolt and the siege of Jerusalem.
Biography of his father-in-law; conquest of Britain to Mons Graupius (83/84).
Ethnography of the Germans.

sources.reliability: The greatest Roman historian; used the acta senatus, memoirs (Agrippina the Younger, Corbulo) and earlier historians (Pliny, Cluvius Rufus, Fabius Rusticus). Reliable on facts, but shapes them with insinuation and a bleak senatorial view of the principate (Tiberius' 'dissimulation'). The Lyon tablet allows comparison of his version of Claudius' speech with the original.
sources.summary: Senator from Gallia Narbonensis or Cisalpina; consul suffect 97, proconsul of Asia c. 112-113.

sources.name: Suetonius

works.books: 12 lives, Julius Caesar to Domitian; the opening of the Julius is lost
works.note: Organized by rubric (family, career, vices, death, omens) rather than chronology.
De grammaticis et rhetoribus survives; lives of Terence, Horace, Lucan and others in excerpt.

sources.reliability: As ab epistulis under Hadrian (dismissed c. 122) he quoted Augustus' letters and other archival documents; gossip-rich and unsystematic, but much detail is genuine. Later lives thinner after loss of archive access.
sources.summary: Equestrian scholar, protégé of Pliny the Younger.

sources.name: Plutarch

works.books: 22 pairs plus 4 single lives survive; the Epaminondas-Scipio pair is lost
works.note: Roman lives: Publicola, Coriolanus, Camillus, Fabius Maximus, Marcellus, Aemilius Paullus, Cato the Elder, Flamininus, Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus, Marius, Sulla, Sertorius, Lucullus, Crassus, Pompey, Caesar, Cato the Younger, Cicero, Brutus, Antony; plus Romulus and Numa (legendary), and Pyrrhus, Philopoemen, Demetrius among Greek subjects of Roman relevance.
Augustus to Vitellius; only Galba and Otho survive.

sources.reliability: Moral biographer who disclaims writing history (Alex. 1), but read widely (Polybius, Posidonius, Fenestella, memoirs of Sulla, letters of Cicero, Asinius Pollio) and preserves much lost material. Chronology loose; character over cause.
sources.summary: Priest at Delphi from Chaeronea; Roman citizen with consular friends (Sosius Senecio).

sources.name: Appian

works.note: Roman wars in Spain to Numantia (133), with a brief note on Augustus' Cantabrian war.
Unique full narrative of the Third Punic War and the siege of Carthage, from Polybius.
To Octavian's Illyrian war (35-33).
War with Antiochus III and a Seleucid history to Pompey.
The only continuous narrative of 133-70 BC; ends with the death of Sextus Pompey.

works.t: Lost books (Kings, Italy, Samnites, Celts, Sicily, Macedonia, Egypt, Dacia, Arabia)

sources.reliability: Arranged by region rather than chronology; his Civil Wars book 1 is the main source for the Gracchan land crisis and Sulla. Reliability depends on lost sources (Polybius, perhaps Asinius Pollio); careless in places but often uniquely informative.
sources.summary: Alexandrian Greek who rose to procurator under Antoninus Pius through Fronto's patronage.

sources.name: Florus

works.note: Rome's wars in biological stages (infancy to old age), to Augustus and Varus.

sources.reliability: Rhetorical summary chiefly from Livy; few independent facts, many errors, but sometimes reflects lost Livian books.
sources.summary: Probably the African-born poet friend of Hadrian.

sources.name: Arrian

works.note: Report to Hadrian as legate of Cappadocia on the Black Sea forts.

works.t: Ektaxis kata Alanon (Order of battle against the Alans)
works.note: His own battle orders for repelling the Alans, unique evidence for a legionary phalanx deployed against cavalry.
Includes the Hadrianic cavalry exercises (hippika gymnasia).
Trajan's Parthian war.

sources.reliability: A serving governor's documents on frontier command; his Anabasis of Alexander is the best source on Alexander.
sources.summary: From Nicomedia; pupil of Epictetus; consul c. 129; legate of Cappadocia 131-137.

sources.name: Gaius

works.books: 4 books; the only classical legal text surviving almost intact, from a Verona palimpsest found by Niebuhr in 1816
works.note: Persons, things, obligations, actions; model for Justinian's Institutes.

sources.reliability: Primary statement of classical private law (status of slaves, freedmen, Latins, peregrines, women's guardianship, the formulary system).
sources.summary: Jurist of the Antonine age, possibly in the East.

sources.name: Cassius Dio

works.books: 80 books; books 36-60 (69 BC-AD 46) survive, with 55-60 partly only in epitome; parts of 78-80 (216-220) in a Vatican codex
works.note: The only continuous narrative for 46-229 apart from Herodian, via the epitomes.
Covers books 36-80; the books on Antoninus Pius and early Marcus were already missing in Xiphilinus' copy.
Zonaras follows Dio for books 1-21 (to 146 BC) and 44-80; between he used Plutarch.
10th-century thematic excerpts (on embassies, virtues and vices, sententiae).

sources.reliability: Senatorial historian writing c. 202-229; eyewitness of Commodus to Severus Alexander (he watched Commodus in the arena). Strongly structural (the Agrippa-Maecenas debate of book 52 as a blueprint for monarchy); reliable on institutions, uneven on the Republic.
sources.summary: From Nicaea in Bithynia, son of a consular; consul c. 205 and (ordinarius, with Severus Alexander) 229; governed Africa, Dalmatia, Pannonia Superior.

sources.name: Herodian

works.t: History of the Empire after Marcus

sources.reliability: Contemporary but vague: few names or dates, rhetorical set-pieces, invented speeches. Independent value for 222-238 (Severus Alexander, Maximinus, the Gordians), where Dio fails.
sources.summary: Probably a Syrian Greek in minor imperial service.

sources.name: Dexippus

works.note: Gothic wars. A palimpsest in Vienna (Scythica Vindobonensia, published 2014) adds Decius' campaigns of 250-251 and an attack on Thessalonica (c. 262).

sources.reliability: Eyewitness of the Herulian sack of Athens (267/268), whose resistance he claimed to have led (IG II2 3669). Used by Zosimus, Zonaras and the HA.
sources.summary: Athenian archon and priest.

sources.name: Historia Augusta

works.books: 30 biographies of emperors, heirs and usurpers from Hadrian to Carinus, ascribed to six authors
works.note: A lacuna removes 244-260 (Philip to the start of Valerian).

sources.reliability: A late-4th-century hoax by a single author (Dessau 1889) posing as six Diocletianic-Constantinian writers. The early 'major' lives (Hadrian to Caracalla) rest on a good lost source (Marius Maximus or the 'Ignotus'); the secondary lives and everything after 238 contain invented documents, people and letters. Use only with control from other sources.
sources.summary: Probably written c. 395-400, possibly by a pagan senator.

sources.name: Vindolanda tablets

works.books: Over 1,700 ink leaf-tablets and stylus tablets, found from 1973 at the fort of Vindolanda behind Hadrian's Wall
works.note: Mostly periods 2-4 (c. 92-105), the cohors IX Batavorum and cohors I Tungrorum.

sources.reliability: Unfiltered military documents: a strength report of the First Tungrians (752 men on the books, only 296 present at Vindolanda, 31 of them unfit), Claudia Severa's birthday invitation (the earliest known Latin in a woman's hand), the disparaging 'Brittunculi', supply accounts.
sources.summary: Written by the garrison and families of the fort before Hadrian's Wall.

sources.name: Oxyrhynchus papyri

works.books: Over 500,000 fragments from the city's rubbish dumps, excavated by Grenfell and Hunt from 1896; 87 volumes published by 2023
works.note: Documentary: census returns, tax receipts, contracts, petitions, letters, imperial edicts, libelli of the Decian sacrifice (250). Literary: lost works (Hellenica Oxyrhynchia, the Livy epitome P.Oxy. 668).

sources.reliability: The densest documentation of any Roman provincial community: prices, wages, liturgies and the working of government from the Ptolemies to the Arab conquest.
sources.summary: Middle Egyptian nome capital (Pemje, modern el-Bahnasa).
